title: Learning to Reason for Factuality
claim: Existing tasks get simple verifiable or judge-based rewards; open-ended generation needs a composite reward that combines several complementary signals.
layout: 2 stacked panels, top existing rewards, bottom ours flowing left-to-right with a combining formula
description: The figure has two dashed-border regions stacked vertically. The top region is labeled 'Verifiable Reward' and 'Human/AI Feedback', with the vertical label 'Existing Task Rewards'. It has four gray sub-panels (Math, Coding, Short-form QA, Instruction Following). Each shows prompt, answer and prediction boxes feeding down through a blue rounded checker (Symbolic Equivalence Checker, Python Interpreter, Exact Match/F1, Reward Model/LLM-as-a-Judge) into a scalar reward box. The bottom region, 'Long-Form Factuality Reward (Ours)', shows a prompt and a long prediction about Apollo 13 feeding into two blue modules, VeriScore and LLM-as-a-Judge. These branch into Factual Precision F/(T+1), Detail Level log(1+F) and Answer Relevance, which are weighted by λ and μ into a final reward of 0.78. Blue labels and blue modules guide the eye.
caption: Reward design for Long-Form Factuality (bottom). Unlike other tasks (top), the factuality of long-form responses cannot be reliably assessed by rule-based heuristics or an LLM judge. Relying solely on automatic evaluation methods such as VeriScore may lead to less detailed or relevant responses. We propose a new reward design that simultaneously considers factual precision, response detail level, and answer relevance (Section [ref]).
abstract: Reasoning Large Language Models (R-LLMs) have significantly advanced complex reasoning tasks but often struggle with factuality, generating substantially more hallucinations than their non-reasoning counterparts on long-form factuality benchmarks. However, extending online Reinforcement Learning (RL), a key component in recent R-LLM advancements, to the long-form factuality setting poses several unique challenges due to the lack of reliable verification methods. Previous work has utilized automatic factuality evaluation frameworks such as FActScore to curate preference data in the offline RL setting, yet we find that directly leveraging such methods as the reward in online RL leads to reward hacking in multiple ways, such as producing less detailed or relevant responses. We propose a novel reward function that simultaneously considers the factual precision, response detail level, and answer relevance, and applies online RL to learn high quality factual reasoning. Evaluated on six long-form factuality benchmarks, our factual reasoning model achieves an average reduction of 23.1 percentage points in hallucination rate, a 23% increase in answer detail level, and no degradation in the overall response helpfulness.
